- `.md` 里的裸 HTML 内的 Markdown 不会渲染；要渲染的示例用 MDX/组件/`aside`，并自己保留边框面板。

## 控件

- 原生 `<select>` 的弹层与 hover 行由系统/浏览器绘制，CSS 控不了；所以主题/语言菜单是自定义列表（`ThemeSelect` / `LanguageSelect`）。
- 列表的「当前值」和「hover」要分开：当前值由触发器文字表达；列表静止态同色，只有 hover 变强调色。
- 移动端把菜单收进 header 的图标 + caret，别让长语言名撑爆导航。
- **splash 页面没有移动菜单**：Starlight 的 header 右组是 `sl-hidden md:sl-flex`，手机上默认整组消失；docs 页有汉堡菜单（菜单里包含主题/语言），splash 页没有，于是主题/语言在手机上不可达。修法（`menu.css` 已带）：仅在**没有** `starlight-menu-button` 的页面把右组放回来，并用 icon-only 触发器。注意菜单按钮在 `nav.sidebar` 里、**不在 header 内**，所以判据挂在 `body` 上：
  `body:not(:has(starlight-menu-button)) header.header .right-group { display: flex; }`
- 组件依赖 `menu.css`；只拷 `.astro` 不拷 CSS，菜单就是裸列表。

## 构建与搜索

- Pagefind 在部分 Windows 环境没有可用二进制；小站直接 `pagefind: false`，`audit` 会记 `PAGEFIND_DISABLED`（info）。
- 自定义 `404` 与 Starlight 的 404 路由可能冲突；要么 `disable404Route: true` 接受没有 404 页，要么自己接管。`audit` 会报 `NOT_FOUND_MISSING`（info）。
- `trailingSlash: 'always'` 让路由集合稳定；改这个值要同步所有手写链接。

## skill 自身

- **不要用 `process.cwd()` 定位 `assets/` / `references/`**：skill 会被复制到别的仓库或全局目录。一律 `fileURLToPath(new URL('../assets/...', import.meta.url))`。
- **不要在 skill 目录下拆第二个给模型调用的 `.js` 入口**：模型只认 `scripts/site.mjs`，`lib/` 只被 import。
- `emit-check` 产物是**一次性快照**：不读 skill、不读配置；改完 skill 必须重导。文件头有「勿手改」标记。
- `check.mjs` 必须只依赖 Node 内置模块、不 import 相对路径，否则 `emit-check` 无法把它渲染成自包含脚本。
- 复制 skill 到新位置后，先在新位置跑一次 `detect`：路径假设与 `assets/` 完整性是唯一的失败点。

---
title: Compatibility & 1.x
description: Host and runtime support, what 1.x promises not to break, and what is explicitly out of scope.
---

## Support matrix

| Surface | Status |
|---|---|
| OpenCode V2 | Supported. 1.1.0 was accepted on host **2.0.32** (Windows and Linux); 1.2.x was re-checked on host **2.2.0** (Windows) in a new process, including concurrent write actions. |
| OpenCode V1 | Not targeted; not tested. |
| Windows | Verified, including new-process end-to-end runs. |
| Linux | Verified, including new-process end-to-end runs. |
| Node.js | **18 or newer** (the plugin runs inside the host). |
| Runtime dependencies | None. Pure Node built-ins. |
| Shell commands | None. |
| Plugin structure | One file. |

## The 1.x compatibility promise

Within 1.x, the following do not change in a breaking way:

1. The four actions (`list`, `inspect`, `disable`, `enable`) and their input fields.
2. The **JSON result envelope**: `schemaVersion`, `action`, `ok`, `warnings`, and the action
   fields documented for 1.1.0. New fields may be added; existing ones are not removed or
   repurposed.
3. The shape of the written rule:
   `{ "action": "skill", "resource": <id>, "effect": "deny" | "ask" }`.
4. The same-line marker comment format (`// skill_management`). `enable` uses it to establish
   provenance after a sidecar loss.
5. The single-file plugin structure.

**1.1.0 is a breaking release.** It replaced the 1.0.0 Markdown output with one JSON object per
call. That is the only breaking change since 1.0.0: the actions, input fields, rule shape,
marker format and file layout are unchanged.

Message wording is not part of the contract. In 1.1.0 the human-readable strings inside
`warnings`, `message`, `conclusion.message` and `error.message` are Chinese. The stable part is
the envelope, the field names, and the literal values (ids, effects, rule JSON, paths).

## What "supported" does not mean

- **Project-level config is out of scope.** A project can contain its own permissions. This
  plugin reads and writes only the global config, and reports the global target file in
  `config.file`.
- **`policies` are out of scope.** The plugin context has no `config` domain, so it cannot read
  policy documents. If a policy blocks a skill, `enable` reports that and stops.
- **Agent-level rules are read, not edited.** They appear in `inspect.agents[]`, and they can
  override a global rule for one agent. That is reported honestly, not "fixed".
- **Host registry internals are internal.** The plugin reads `ctx.skill` / `ctx.agent` through
  the host's transform API and consumes `{ location, data }` envelopes where required. A host
  change to those shapes is a compatibility event, not something the plugin can paper over.
- **No network access.** The plugin never calls out, and the docs site has no analytics, no
  cookies, and no language-based redirect.

## How this release was verified

- `node tools/verify.mjs`: **333 assertions** in sections A–J, run entirely against a temporary
  config directory (no real user config touched). Section E parses every result and validates it
  against the declared `output` contract.
- The same harness runs on `ubuntu-latest` and `windows-latest` in CI.
- End-to-end checks run in a **new process**, because plugins load at host startup.
- Section H is a performance gate: `list` under 25 ms at 29 skills × 12 agents × 10 rules.
- Section I is a release gate: pack contents, resolvable `exports`, and byte-identical installed
  copy.

Full details, plus the Linux/WSL acceptance script, are on
[Development & verification](../development/).

Those checks are about the plugin. The documentation site is built separately with Astro and
Starlight and deployed to GitHub Pages.

## Upgrading

- Patch releases fix behavior without changing the interfaces above.
- Minor releases may add output fields, but not remove or repurpose existing ones. 1.1.0 is the
  documented exception: the Markdown output was replaced by JSON.
- If a host upgrade changes registry or reload behavior, the plugin will report "unverified"
  rather than invent a conclusion. Check the issue tracker before assuming silence means
  support.

## Version

The current release is **1.2.1**. The npm package is `opencode-skill-management`; the
repository is [sogeisetsu/opencode-skill-management](https://github.com/sogeisetsu/opencode-skill-management).
Licensed MIT.

---
title: Design decisions
description: Why the plugin writes permission rules instead of policies, why there is no "allow", why it edits text instead of rewriting JSON, and what each choice costs.
---

`skill_management` is deliberately small: four actions, one rule shape, one file it may write.
This page records the choices behind that surface, the evidence for them, and — for each one —
what the alternative would have bought and what this choice gives up.

## Why a `permissions` rule, not a `policies` entry

OpenCode has two ways to stop a skill from being used:

| Mechanism | What it removes | Granularity | Writable by this plugin |
|---|---|---|---|
| `permissions` rule with `effect: "deny"` | The skill from the model-visible list, and loading is rejected | One skill id, **per agent** | Yes |
| `policies` (`integration.use` deny) | The skill from the registry itself | One integration id, globally | No |

A permission rule is used because it is the only mechanism that expresses all three states this
tool needs to distinguish: `allow`, `deny` and `ask`. `ask` is a native `Permission.Effect`, not a
workaround — the host keeps the skill listed and asks at load time. Rules are also evaluated
against each agent's own rule set, so the tool can answer a per-agent question ("is this available
to *me*?") instead of a global one.

**The cost.** A `policies` deny is more thorough: it takes the skill out of the registry
(`s.remove(id)`), so it disappears for every agent and even from tools that read the registry
directly. This plugin cannot match that, and cannot read policy documents either: the plugin
context has no `config` domain. If a policy is what blocked a skill, `enable` reports it and stops.

Choose a policy when the skill must not exist at all for anyone. Choose a permission rule when you
want a switch that is visible, per-agent and reversible.

## Why there is no `allow`

`disable` only ever appends `deny` or `ask`; `enable` only deletes a rule with one of those
effects.

An appended `allow` would take priority over every earlier rule for that id, including a broader
`deny` that someone wrote on purpose. That silently widens the blast radius: the tool would be
"fixing" one skill by overriding a decision it never made. It would also break the ownership
model: `enable` recognises the rules it wrote by effect and marker, so a self-written `allow`
would be a rule nobody ever reclaims.

**The cost.** Re-enabling is always a deletion, never an override. When an agent-level rule or a
wildcard `deny` still blocks the skill afterwards, the tool reports it and leaves it alone; you
edit that rule yourself.

## Why only the global config

There is exactly one write target, resolved in a documented order (see
[Permissions & evaluation](../permissions/#which-config-file-is-written)). Project configs,
`agents.<id>.permissions` and `policies` are read or reported, never edited.

One target means the tool can be honest about what it changed: `config.file` names it, a backup is
taken from it, and `enable` looks for the rule there first. It also means no surprise edits in a
repository you happen to be in.

**The cost.** You cannot disable a skill for one project only, and you cannot disable it for one
agent only. Both are real use cases; both are out of scope.

## Why minimal text edits, with a same-line marker

The global config is usually hand-maintained JSONC: comments, key order, indentation, CRLF/LF and
sometimes a BOM. Parsing it into an object and serialising it back would destroy all of that, so
the plugin inserts or removes the single item as text, then validates the result before writing.

The `// skill_management` trailing comment is provenance that lives *inside* the file. It survives
a lost or corrupt sidecar, and it is the first thing `enable` looks for. Its format is part of the
1.x compatibility promise, because deleting a rule after a sidecar loss depends on it.

**The cost.** The writer must keep producing that exact marker forever. And if another tool strips
comments from your config, the marker is gone — `enable` then falls back to the sidecar record, or
refuses rather than guessing.

## Why writes are serialized

The host can run several tool calls from one step **concurrently**. Two write actions racing on the
same file interleave read → edit → verify → record, and the later rollback can write the earlier
change back: the file ends up holding a rule that should not exist.

Every `disable` / `enable` runs inside an in-process queue now, so the second call starts only after
the first — including its read-back polling — has finished, and therefore reads the first call's
result.

**The cost.** A second write waits instead of being rejected, and verification can take several
seconds, so a concurrent call is delayed by that much. The queue is per host process: two separate
OpenCode processes editing the same config can still overwrite each other, which is outside what a
plugin can lock.

## Why the sidecar is only an audit trail

`<config>/skill_management.state.json` records id, effect, file and timestamp for rules this tool
wrote. It is never replayed: when it disagrees with the config, `list` reports the mismatch and the
config wins.

**The cost.** If both the marker and the sidecar record are lost, `enable` cannot prove the rule is
the tool's, and it prints the rule instead of deleting it. Writing the sidecar is best-effort too:
if it cannot be saved, the config change still counts as done, and the result says so in `warnings`
with `sidecar: null`.

## Choosing the mechanism for your case

| What you want | Use |
|---|---|
| The skill gone for everyone, as if it were never installed | `policies` (`integration.use` deny) |
| Hidden from the model and refused at load, per agent | `disable` (a `permissions` rule with `effect: "deny"`) |
| Listed, but every load asks for confirmation | `disable` with `effect: "ask"` |
| Never injected into context, but still loadable by name | `disable-model-invocation` in `SKILL.md` — frontmatter, not a permission; this tool only reports it |

Next: [Development & verification](../development/) for how these behaviours are tested.

---
title: Development & verification
description: The acceptance harness, its sections and gates, the CI matrix, what goes into the npm package, and why two copies of the plugin cannot coexist.
---

There is no test framework and no build step. The whole acceptance suite is one Node script that
runs against a temporary config directory.

## Run the harness

```pwsh
node tools/verify.mjs                # all sections, 333 assertions
node tools/verify.mjs --section E    # one section (A–J, by title prefix, case-insensitive)
node tools/verify.mjs --keep         # keep the temporary directory for inspection
```

Every run creates a fresh `mkdtemp` directory and points `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` at it, so the real
global config is never read or written. The installer step gets its own temporary
`XDG_CONFIG_HOME` as well, and `OPENCODE_CONFIG` / `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` are cleared for it so a
running instance's npm channel cannot be mistaken for an installed one.

## Sections

| Section | Covers |
|---|---|
| A | Module shape and purity: default export, four actions, only `node:` imports, no third-party dependencies, no shell or `eval` |
| B | `globMatch` and permission evaluation: last match wins, `ask` fallback on no match |
| C | Id derivation from paths, source classification, `user` / `project` scope |
| D | JSONC text edits: insert, remove, create the block, CRLF, BOM, comments preserved, strict validation, failure paths |
| D2 | Target config resolution under a fake `env` / `home`: XDG, home, two candidates, two directories |
| E | End-to-end on a temporary config: `list`, `inspect`, `dryRun`, `disable`, `enable`, backup, sidecar, read-back verification, refusal branches, concurrent writes against the same file, and `OUTPUT_SCHEMA` validation of every action's `output` |
| F | Id derivation from the registry (§3.5) and the ownership boundary of `enable` |
| G | Read-back criteria, one backup, atomic write, description hardening |
| H | Performance gate |
| I | Release gate |
| J | Installer conflict detection |

Section E parses every result and checks it against the declared `output` schema — required
fields, property types, `error.code` / `error.message` — and asserts that `content` is the same
data as `output`. Its negative cases keep that validator honest: a `null` where a string is
declared, or a string where a boolean is declared, must be reported.

## Linux / WSL

```bash
bash tools/linux-verify.sh      # KEEP=1 to keep the scratch directory
```

This script is a real-host acceptance, not a unit run. It downloads its own Node and
`@opencode/cli` (pinned by `NODE_VERSION` / `OPENCODE_VERSION`), runs the harness on a copy of the
repository, then loads the plugin in a temporary `HOME` and checks `opencode plugin list
--builtin`. It needs `curl`, `tar` and `gzip`, uses no `sudo`, and deletes its scratch directory on
exit. It also snapshots the real `~/.config/opencode` and `~/.local/share/opencode` before and
after, and fails if they changed.

## CI

`.github/workflows/verify.yml` runs `node tools/verify.mjs` on `ubuntu-latest` and
`windows-latest` with Node 22. The suite needs no secrets: it never touches a real config.
`.github/workflows/pages.yml` builds the documentation site and runs `npm run docs:check`, which
fails on a missing route, an en/zh route mismatch, a dead internal link, a link outside the base
path, or a language switcher that does not point at the mirrored page.

## The two gates

**H — performance.** 29 skills × 12 agents × 10 rules, best of five `list` calls must stay under
25 ms. The threshold is deliberately loose so CI jitter does not produce false failures; it exists
to catch an accidental O(n²) or a re-parse per skill.

**I — release.** `npm pack --dry-run` must contain the entry file, the pack must not contain
`tools/`, `docs/`, CI or repository docs, `exports["."]` must resolve through the package name, and
an installed single-file copy must be byte-identical to `src/skill_management.js`.

## What is in the npm package

Five files, nothing else:

```text
package.json
README.md
CHANGELOG.md
LICENSE
src/skill_management.js
```

`package.json` lists `files: ["src", "CHANGELOG.md"]`; npm adds `package.json`, `README.md` and
`LICENSE`. Tests, the docs site, CI and the design specification stay in the repository.

## Why the plugin is one file

The host loads every `.js` and `.ts` file in `<config>/plugins/`, including subdirectories, as a
plugin. Splitting helper modules out of `skill_management.js` would create a second plugin whose
validation fails. The distributed plugin therefore stays a single file, and
`tools/install.mjs` copies that exact file.

For the same reason, two copies cannot coexist. With both an npm entry and
`<config>/plugins/skill_management.js`, the host reports `Duplicate plugin ID: skill_management`
and one of them shows as failed — it is not "both work, one is ignored". Move between channels with
`node tools/install.mjs --uninstall` (to npm) or `opencode plugin remove
opencode-skill-management` (back to the single file), and use `node tools/install.mjs --check` to
see both sources before changing anything.

Next: [Design decisions](../design-decisions/) for why these behaviours are the ones being tested.

---
title: Installation
description: Three ways to load the plugin (npm, git spec, single file) and how to verify it loaded.
---

The plugin is one JavaScript file with no third-party runtime dependencies. Pick whichever
channel fits your setup; all three result in the same code.

## Requirements

- OpenCode **V2**. 1.1.0 was accepted on host 2.0.32 on Windows and Linux; 1.2.x was re-checked on
  host 2.2.0, including a new-process end-to-end run.
- Node.js **18 or newer** in the environment that runs OpenCode.
- No token, registry account or build step is needed.

## Channel 1 — npm (recommended)

```pwsh
opencode plugin add opencode-skill-management
```

This is the channel to pick unless you have a reason not to: one command installs the package and
registers it in the global config, and the host handles upgrades (`opencode plugin check` /
`opencode plugin update`). The package exports exactly one entry point:
`./src/skill_management.js`. Runtime dependencies: none.

## Channel 2 — git spec

```pwsh
opencode plugin add github:sogeisetsu/opencode-skill-management
```

OpenCode fetches the repository directly. No npm registry and no publish step are involved; the
same host commands handle upgrades.

## Channel 3 — copy the single file (no updates)

Use this when neither network channel fits (offline machine, vendored setup):

```pwsh
node tools/install.mjs          # copies to <config>/plugins/skill_management.js
node tools/install.mjs --check  # report only: path, version, conflicts
```

This channel is **pinned**: the file you install stays until you run the installer again. It does
not follow npm releases, and upgrading means re-running `node tools/install.mjs`. If you want
updates to arrive on their own, use channel 1 or 2 — `opencode plugin check` and
`opencode plugin update` handle those.

`<config>` resolves the way the host resolves it: `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR`, then
`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode`, then `~/.config/opencode` (on Windows,
`C:\Users\<you>\.config\opencode`).

Before writing anything the installer looks for a second source. If `opencode.json(c)` already
lists this package in `plugins`, or another copy sits in `plugins/`, it refuses to write and exits
with code `2`, leaving every file untouched.

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--check` / `--dry-run` | Report only, never write |
| `--uninstall` | Delete `<config>/plugins/skill_management.js` and nothing else (refuses if the file is not this plugin) |
| `--npm` | Assert the npm channel is installed; never write; exits `1` when it is missing |
| `--force` | Write anyway (creates two copies; the host reports `Duplicate plugin ID` for one of them) |
| `--json` | Machine-readable output |
| `--help` / `-h` | Print usage and exit `0`; writes nothing |

Unknown flags exit with code `3`; nothing is written.

OpenCode loads every `.js` and `.ts` file in `<config>/plugins/`, plus subdirectories. You do
not register the file in `opencode.jsonc`.

:::caution[Keep the plugin directory single-file]
Because every file in `plugins/` is loaded as a plugin, do not split `skill_management` into
helper modules or drop a second copy beside it. The distributed plugin is intentionally one
file for this reason.
:::

:::caution[One plugin, one channel]
A plugin id can only be loaded once. With both the npm entry and
`<config>/plugins/skill_management.js` present, the host reports
`Duplicate plugin ID: skill_management` and one of them shows as failed — the two do not simply
coexist. Moving to npm: run `node tools/install.mjs --uninstall` first. Moving back to the single
file: run `opencode plugin remove opencode-skill-management` first. `node tools/install.mjs --check`
lists both sources and the exact command to run.
:::

## Verify that it loaded

```pwsh
opencode plugin list --builtin
```

`--builtin` matters. Without it, plugins loaded from the local directory are not listed and you
may see `No plugins found`.

The output should contain a `skill_management` entry: source `local` for the single-file
channel, or the package source for npm / git spec. In a brand-new config directory, the first one or two calls can be
empty; run it again.

Then ask the model to call the tool, or call it yourself:

```text
skill_management({ action: "list" })
```

The `list` result — `config.file` and the `skills[]` array — is enough to confirm that the
plugin is reading the host registries.

## Notes on loading

- Plugins load when the OpenCode process starts. A newly added plugin appears in the next
  process, not in an already running one.
- `skill_management` is registered as a **native tool** with `codemode: false`. Call it by name.
  It is not present in the Code Mode `search()` / `execute()` catalog, and "not found there" does
  not mean it failed to install.
- The tool writes only to the global config. It never writes project configuration.

Once installed, continue with the [overview](../overview/) or go straight to the
[`list` action](../actions/list/).

---
title: Overview
description: What opencode-skill-management does, why it uses permission rules, and what it deliberately refuses to touch.
---

`opencode-skill-management` is a single-file OpenCode V2 plugin. It adds one native tool,
`skill_management`, with four actions: `list`, `inspect`, `disable` and `enable`.

It does not install, delete, move or rewrite skills. It reads the host's live registries and,
when you ask it to change something, writes **one exact permission rule** to the global OpenCode
config.

## The problems it solves

**The skill list becomes noise.** Every installed skill contributes a name and description to
the model's context. Once the list is long, the useful entries are harder to find and every
turn pays for the rest.

**A broken skill is opaque.** A skill can be registered and still be refused at load time. The
interesting question is not "is it installed?" but "which rule matched, for this agent, right
now?" — and that answer usually requires reading three config layers.

**Turning one off is disproportionate.** Renaming a directory or editing `SKILL.md` works, but
it is a real file change that you have to remember to undo. A permission rule is smaller,
inspectable and reversible.

## The model

OpenCode evaluates skill permissions as a list of rules, last match wins, with glob matching.
The plugin treats a rule as the only state it owns:

```jsonc
{ "action": "skill", "resource": "windows-shell", "effect": "deny" } // skill_management
```

- `disable` appends exactly this rule to the global config.
- `enable` removes exactly this rule.
- Both verify the result by asking the host to reload and then re-reading the caller agent's
  effective rule set. A write that the host did not pick up is rolled back, not reported as
  success.

The rest of the design follows from that:

| Property | Consequence |
|---|---|
| No skill file is touched | Nothing to restore if you change your mind |
| Rules are evaluated per agent | `list` reports the caller's state, not a merged global view |
| No match means `ask` | An `ask` state may mean "explicitly soft-disabled" or "no rule matched"; `inspect` distinguishes them |
| Global config only | Project-level config, `policies` and agent-level rules are reported, never edited |

:::note[Output format]
Every action returns one JSON object: `schemaVersion`, `action`, `ok`, `warnings`, plus the
action-specific fields described on these pages. Human-readable strings inside `warnings`,
`message`, `conclusion.message` and `error.message` are Chinese in 1.2.x; field names and
literal values are stable.
:::

## A first session

These are **tool calls**, not shell commands: each line is the argument object passed to the
native `skill_management` tool.

```text title="tool calls"
skill_management({ action: "list" })
skill_management({ action: "inspect", id: "windows-shell" })
skill_management({ action: "disable", id: "windows-shell", dryRun: true })
skill_management({ action: "disable", id: "windows-shell" })
skill_management({ action: "enable",  id: "windows-shell" })
```

`list` is read-only and safe to run at any time. `dryRun` on either write action returns the
exact lines in `diff` and writes nothing.

## What it will not do

- Edit, move, delete or reinstall a skill, or touch `SKILL.md` frontmatter.
- Write project-level configuration.
- Write `policies` or `experimental.policies`.
- Edit agent-level `agents.<id>.permissions`.
- Write `opencode.managed.json` (the second global config used by OpenChamber).
- Delete a rule it cannot uniquely identify. It prints the candidate and stops.
- Claim a rule "took effect" when an agent-level rule still overrides it.

## Next

- [Install it](../installation/) through one of three channels.
- Learn each action: [list](../actions/list/), [inspect](../actions/inspect/),
  [disable](../actions/disable/), [enable](../actions/enable/).
- Read the [permission evaluation model](../permissions/) before editing rules by hand.

---
title: Permissions & evaluation
description: The rule shape, last-match-wins evaluation, the ask fallback, agent-level overrides, and which file the plugin is allowed to write.
---

Everything `skill_management` changes is a permission rule. Reading this page is enough to
predict what the tool will report before you run it.

## The rule

```jsonc
{ "action": "skill", "resource": "windows-shell", "effect": "deny" } // skill_management
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `action` | The permission action. Skill permissions use the literal `skill`. |
| `resource` | The skill id. Exact id, or a glob pattern. |
| `effect` | `allow`, `deny` or `ask`. |

Rules live in the **top-level `permissions` array** of the global config. This is the V2 form:

```jsonc
{
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "skill", "resource": "windows-shell", "effect": "deny" }
  ]
}
```

:::caution[`permissions` vs `permission`]
The plural `permissions` (an array) is the V2 field used by this plugin. The singular
`permission` (an object) is deprecated. If you only have the singular field, this plugin will not
find or edit it.
:::

## Evaluation

The host evaluates the caller agent's rule set from the **end to the beginning** and takes the
first match. Equivalently: the **last matching rule wins**. Both `action` and `resource` are
matched as globs (`*` and `?`).

```text
rules[0] { action: "skill", resource: "*",             effect: "allow" }
rules[1] { action: "skill", resource: "windows-shell", effect: "deny"  }

→ windows-shell is denied (rules[1] is later)
```

Consequences:

- **Order is part of the semantics.** Appending a rule gives it priority over earlier rules in
  the same array. `disable` appends.
- **A broad rule can beat a specific one** if it comes later. `inspect` calls this out; adding
  another rule for the same id would not fix it.
- **There is no implicit allow.** When nothing matches, the host falls back to **`ask`**, not
  `allow`.

```text
no matching rule  →  ask
```

That fallback is why `ask` is ambiguous:

| What you see | Possible cause |
|---|---|
| `ask` | An explicit `{ action: "skill", resource: "<id>", effect: "ask" }` rule matched. |
| `ask` | No rule matched at all; the host fell back to `ask`. |

`list` shows `ask` for both. [`inspect`](../actions/inspect/) distinguishes them by reporting
`命中 rules[i]` or `无规则命中 → 回退 ask`.

## Effects

| Effect | Model-visible skill list | Loading through the `skill` tool |
|---|---|---|
| `allow` | Listed | Allowed |
| `ask` | Listed | Asks for confirmation |
| `deny` | Hidden | Rejected (`permission.rejected`) |

### deny vs ask

Both stop a skill from being loaded silently, but they stop it in different places.

| | `deny` | `ask` |
|---|---|---|
| Model-visible list | Hidden | Still listed, still described |
| Load attempt | Rejected (`permission.rejected`) | Blocks on a confirmation |
| Interrupts the turn | No — it just fails | Yes — someone has to answer |
| Who can override | A later rule in the caller's own rule set (e.g. an agent-level `allow`), or a `policies` entry | A later rule in the caller's own rule set |
| Typical use | A skill you do not want in context at all | A skill that is fine to use, but not on its own initiative |

`ask` is not simply a softer `deny`. It does **not** reduce the probability that the model tries to
use the skill: the skill is still in the list, still described, still a candidate. What `ask` buys
is a decision point; what it costs is an interruption.

Three real cases, and the reasoning that picks an effect:

| Skill | Why it needs a switch | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `codebuddy-second-opinion` | Shells out to another model and spends quota/credits | `ask` — useful when you asked for a second opinion, wasteful when the model decides on its own |
| `disk-clean` | Scans caches and actually deletes files | `ask` for review; `deny` if you never want the model reaching for it |
| `meld-deepresearch` | Network access and long, expensive runs | `deny` — a mistaken invocation costs far more than the convenience is worth |

The granularity is the skill **id**, not an individual file or invocation. A skill whose id does
not exist fails with `Unable to load skill <id>`, which is a different error from a permission
rejection.

## Whose rules are evaluated

Each agent has its own effective rule set. The plugin evaluates only the **calling agent**; it
never merges every agent's rules into one list. Merging is wrong because sub-agents
(`explorer`, `title`, …) carry their own `deny` rules that do not apply to the caller.

A typical divergence: the global config denies a skill, but one agent has its own later `allow`
or vice versa. In that case:

- `list` shows the caller's state and says other **visible** agents differ (hidden internal agents are only listed in `inspect`).
- `inspect` returns the per-agent results in `agents[]`.
- `disable` reports that the rule was written but the caller's actual effect is still different,
  instead of claiming success.

Rules set in `agents.<id>.permissions` are not edited by this tool. They are only reported.

## Which config file is written

The plugin resolves the global config in this order:

1. `<config>` is `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` if that is set, else `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode` if
   `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is set, else `~/.config/opencode`
   (`C:\Users\<you>\.config\opencode` on Windows).
2. Candidates are `opencode.json` and `opencode.jsonc` in `<config>`, plus the same names in
   `~/.config/opencode` when that is a different directory. `opencode.jsonc` is preferred over
   `opencode.json`.
3. If both locations contain a `permissions` array, the plugin picks the `~/.config/opencode`
   file and adds a warning to its output.
4. If no candidate has `permissions`, it uses the last existing candidate, or creates
   `<config>/opencode.jsonc` if none exists.

`opencode.managed.json` is **never** written. That is OpenChamber's second, managed global
config; editing it would fight the host.

## Minimal text edits

The config is not parsed into an object and re-serialized. The plugin inserts or removes the
specific item as text, so comments, indentation, key order, trailing commas and the file's own
CRLF/LF and BOM survive. The result is parsed and validated before it is written.

Writes are atomic: a temp file in the same directory is renamed into place. Before writing, one
backup is saved under `<config>/skill_management.backups/`.

:::danger[Backups contain secrets]
The global config often contains MCP credentials. The backup is a byte-for-byte copy. Do not
paste it into an issue, commit it, or treat it as harmless evidence.
:::

## The sidecar

`<config>/skill_management.state.json` records which rules this tool wrote (id, effect, file,
timestamp). It is a hint, not the source of truth:

- `enable` prefers the in-file marker comment and only falls back to the sidecar.
- If the sidecar and config disagree, `list` reports the mismatch and does not "replay" anything.

The same-line marker is deliberate: it is the only provenance that survives a lost sidecar, and
its format is part of the 1.x compatibility promise.

## Patterns

| Pattern | Matches |
|---|---|
| `windows-shell` | Exactly that id |
| `*` | Every skill |
| `pdf-*` | Ids starting with `pdf-` |
| `?` | Exactly one character |

Prefer exact ids. A wildcard `deny` is reported by `enable` and never deleted automatically,
because deleting it would change more than the one skill you named.

## Hand-written examples

```jsonc
{
  "permissions": [
    // hide one skill completely
    { "action": "skill", "resource": "windows-shell", "effect": "deny" },

    // keep it listed, ask on load
    { "action": "skill", "resource": "pdf-tools", "effect": "ask" }
  ]
}
```

A hand-written rule without the marker can still be removed by `enable` if the sidecar has a
matching record and the rule is unique. Otherwise `enable` prints it for you to remove yourself.

Next: [Troubleshooting & FAQ](../troubleshooting/) for the failure modes in practice.

---
title: Troubleshooting & FAQ
description: Diagnose missing plugins, unexpected ask states, overridden rules, refused enable operations and config mismatches.
---

Start with the action that observes rather than changes: `list`, then `inspect` for the skill
that looks wrong. Almost every question below is answered by the rule quoted in `inspect`.

## The plugin does not appear

**`opencode plugin list --builtin` says `No plugins found`.** Add `--builtin`; without it,
locally loaded plugins are not listed. In a fresh config directory the first one or two calls
can also be empty — run it again.

**The plugin was just installed but is not active.** Plugins load at process start. Restart
OpenCode (or start a new process) and check again.

**Channel 3 was used.** Confirm the destination exists:
`<config>/plugins/skill_management.js`. `<config>` is `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` when set, else
`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode` when set, otherwise `~/.config/opencode`.
`node tools/install.mjs --dry-run` prints the exact path.

**A second file was added to `plugins/`.** Every `.js`/`.ts` file in that directory is loaded as
a plugin. A helper module or a second copy will be loaded too and can fail validation. Keep
`skill_management` as the single file.

## The tool cannot be found by the model

`skill_management` is a native tool with `codemode: false`. It is intentionally absent from the
Code Mode `search()` / `execute()` catalog. A model that checks only that catalog will conclude
"the tool does not exist" and give up. Ask it to call the tool directly by name.

## A skill is installed but cannot be loaded

Run:

```text
skill_management({ action: "inspect", id: "<id>" })
```

The conclusion names the effect and the exact matched rule. Common causes:

- A `deny` rule for the id, possibly written earlier.
- A later broad rule (`resource: "*"`) that denies more than you expected.
- An agent-level rule in `agents.<id>.permissions` that overrides the global config for the
  calling agent.
- The id is wrong: an unknown id produces `Unable to load skill <id>`, which is not a permission
  error.

## `list` says `ask` — is it disabled?

Not necessarily. `ask` has two causes: an explicit rule with `effect: "ask"`, or **no matching
rule**, because the host falls back to `ask`. `inspect` tells them apart:

- `命中 rules[i] = {...}` → an explicit rule.
- `无规则命中 → 回退 ask` → no rule at all.

If you want a skill fully hidden, use `effect: "deny"`, not `"ask"`.

## `disable` said it wrote the rule, but the skill is still available

Read the verification paragraph. The plugin distinguishes three outcomes:

1. **Written and effective for the caller.** The caller's effect is `deny`.
2. **Written, but the caller is still overridden.** The output reports the actual effect,
   usually because that agent has its own later rule. Other agents may see the new rule.
3. **Verification failed.** The original file was restored and the output says it rolled back.

Case 2 is not a bug in the write; it is a rule-order fact. `inspect.agents[]` shows per-agent results.
Remove or change the overriding agent rule yourself — the plugin does not edit agent-level
permissions.

## `disable` changes nothing and says it is already disabled

That is the intended no-op. If a broad rule caused it, the output quotes that rule and explains
that a new per-id rule would be redundant.

## `enable` refuses

Count the reasons:

- **No exact rule for the id.** The blocker is broader (`resource: "*"`), agent-level, or a
  policy. The output quotes it. Edit it by hand.
- **Several candidates.** Two rules for the same id, or two lines carrying the marker. The tool
  will not choose.
- **Neither marker nor sidecar record.** A hand-written rule that the sidecar does not know is
  printed verbatim. Delete it yourself if it is the one you mean.
- **The config cannot be parsed.** Fix the JSONC syntax first. The tool will not edit a document
  it cannot locate items in.
- **The sidecar says one thing, the config another.** `list` reports the mismatch. Run `inspect`
  to see what is actually effective.

## The rule is in the file, but the host did not pick it up

Config reload is asynchronous. `disable` and `enable` already poll for up to six seconds. If
your machine is slower, set `SKILL_MGMT_VERIFY_TIMEOUT_MS` (milliseconds) before starting
OpenCode. A timeout triggers a rollback, so the file will not be left in a half-verified state.

## Which file was edited?

The output prints the resolved target file and the reason it was chosen. The short version:
`opencode.jsonc` beats `opencode.json`, `<config>` is XDG-aware, and a second `permissions`
array under `~/.config/opencode` triggers a warning and that file is preferred.
`opencode.managed.json` is never written. See
[Permissions & evaluation](../permissions/).

## Can I undo a disable?

Yes — `enable` with the same id. It deletes the exact rule. The one backup in
`<config>/skill_management.backups/` is for recovery after a bad write, not a version history.

## Does it delete or modify skills?

No. It does not touch skill files, `SKILL.md` frontmatter, directories, project config,
`policies`, or agent-level permissions. It reads the registries and edits the global
`permissions` array.

## Is the backup safe to share?

No. It is a byte-for-byte copy of a config that commonly contains MCP credentials. Do not commit
it, attach it to an issue, or paste it into chat. When reporting a problem, quote only the
relevant rule (the output of `inspect` already does that).

## `name` matches more than one skill

Use the id. A duplicate name returns the candidate ids rather than picking one. The same applies
to `disable` and `enable`.

## Unknown action

The four actions are `list`, `inspect`, `disable`, `enable`. Anything else returns an error
listing them. The `action` field is required.

## The `list` count differs from what the model sees

`list` counts every registered skill. The model-visible list is filtered per agent and excludes
skills denied for that agent. A `deny` row in `list` is expected to be absent from the model's
view; that is the point of disabling it.

## A path or id looks wrong on Windows

Ids are taken from the registry when present. When absent, they are derived from the path:
`<dir>/SKILL.md` → the directory name, `<dir>/<name>.md` → the file name without `.md`.
`inspect` prints the derivation and the exact path it used. `source` and `scope` are classified
from that path, so unusual symlinks or drive mappings can change the label without changing the
id.

---
title: disable
description: Write one exact global permission rule so a skill is hidden and rejected at load — JSON result, dry run, soft disable, verified rollback.
---

`disable` appends one exact rule to the **global** config:

```jsonc
{ "action": "skill", "resource": "<id>", "effect": "deny" } // skill_management
```

With `deny`, the skill disappears from the model-visible list and the built-in `skill` tool
refuses to load it. With `effect: "ask"`, it stays listed and asks for confirmation.

It never edits, moves or deletes a skill file.

## Parameters

| Name | Type | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `action` | `"disable"` | yes | Selects this action. |
| `id` | string | one of `id` / `name` | Skill id to disable. |
| `name` | string | one of `id` / `name` | Alias, used only when it matches exactly one skill. |
| `effect` | `"deny"` \| `"ask"` | no | Default `deny`. `ask` is a soft disable. |
| `dryRun` | boolean | no | Default `false`. `true` reports the exact changed lines and writes nothing. |

`id` wins over `name`. An ambiguous name returns the candidates instead of picking one; an
unknown id returns near matches. Both are errors, not writes.

```text
skill_management({ action: "disable", id: "windows-shell" })
skill_management({ action: "disable", id: "windows-shell", dryRun: true })
skill_management({ action: "disable", id: "windows-shell", effect: "ask" })
```

## What happens, in order

1. **Resolve the target** through the skill registry (id, or a unique name).
2. **Read the caller's current effect.** If it is already `deny`, nothing is written. If a
   broader rule (for example `resource: "*"`) is responsible, the result quotes it and says
   that a new rule for this id is unnecessary.
3. **Resolve the global config file.** The plugin reads the candidate files, prefers
   `opencode.jsonc` over `opencode.json`, and never writes `opencode.managed.json`. See
   [Permissions & evaluation](../../permissions/) for the full order.
4. **Apply a minimal text edit.** The rule is inserted into the existing `permissions` array
   (created if absent), preserving indentation, key order, line endings (CRLF/LF) and BOM. The
   file is parsed and validated before writing.
5. **Write atomically.** A temp file in the same directory is renamed over the target. If the
   target existed, one backup is kept in `<config>/skill_management.backups/`. The backup is a
   byte-for-byte copy of a file that often contains MCP credentials; treat it as secret.
6. **Reload and verify.** The plugin calls the host's agent reload and polls the caller's rule
   set for up to 6 seconds (`SKILL_MGMT_VERIFY_TIMEOUT_MS` overrides this).
   - For `deny`, the criterion is that the caller's effective effect is `deny`.
   - For `ask`, the criterion is that the number of exact `{skill, id, ask}` rules increased.
     "Not deny" is not accepted: the host's no-match fallback is also `ask`.
7. **Roll back on failure.** If verification fails, the original bytes are restored and the
   result says so. A half-written config is never left behind.
8. **Record provenance.** On success, `<config>/skill_management.state.json` records the id,
   effect, file and timestamp. This sidecar helps `enable` find a rule whose marker comment was
   stripped by another tool.

## What it returns

The usual envelope (`schemaVersion`, `action`, `ok`, `warnings`) plus:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `id`, `effect`, `dryRun` | string, string, boolean | Echo of the resolved request. `effect` is `deny` unless `ask` was passed. |
| `callerAgent` | string \| null | Agent whose rule set was used. |
| `before` | object | `index` and `rule` before the change; `rule` is `null` when nothing matched. |
| `targetFile` | string | Global config file. |
| `configNotes` | string[] | Why that file was chosen. |
| `changed` | boolean | `true` only when the config was actually modified. |
| `reason` | string | Present when `changed` is `false`: `already_disabled` or `covered_by_broader_rule`. |
| `message` | string | The human-readable explanation for a no-op or a `dryRun`. |
| `planned` | boolean | `true` for `dryRun`. |
| `createdBlock` | boolean | Whether a new `permissions` block was created. |
| `diff` | string[] | The exact changed lines that were (or would be) written. |
| `backup` | string \| null | Backup path, when the target existed. |
| `sidecar` | string \| null | Sidecar path written on success; `null` when the sidecar could not be written (the config change still stands and `warnings` explains it). |
| `verification` | object | `ok`, `via`, `caller`, `expected`, `actual`, `beforeCount`, `count`, `diverged`. |

`verification.via` names the reload/poll path and includes the exact-rule count transition
(for example `精确规则数 0→1`), so a rule that the host never read cannot look like success.

When the rule is written and read back but the **caller's** actual effect is still different
(that agent has its own later rule), `verification.actual` differs from `expected` and
`warnings` says the change is not effective for that caller. Divergent agents are listed the
same way. Neither is reported as "applied".

## Example output

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "action": "disable",
  "ok": true,
  "warnings": [],
  "id": "windows-shell",
  "effect": "deny",
  "dryRun": false,
  "callerAgent": "build",
  "before": { "index": 0, "rule": { "action": "*", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" } },
  "targetFile": "<config>\\opencode.jsonc",
  "configNotes": ["目标文件含现有 permissions，直接在其数组中追加/删除"],
  "changed": true,
  "createdBlock": false,
  "diff": ["    { \"action\": \"skill\", \"resource\": \"windows-shell\", \"effect\": \"deny\" } // skill_management"],
  "backup": "<config>\\skill_management.backups\\opencode.jsonc.2026-10-30T01-02-03-456Z.bak",
  "sidecar": "<config>\\skill_management.state.json",
  "verification": {
    "ok": true,
    "via": "ctx.agent.reload() + ctx.agent.list()（轮询 1 次；精确规则数 0→1）",
    "caller": "build",
    "expected": "deny",
    "actual": "deny",
    "beforeCount": 0,
    "count": 1,
    "diverged": []
  }
}
```

## Errors

| `error.code` | When | File touched |
|---|---|---|
| `verification_failed` | The host did not read the rule back in time. `rolledBack: true`; original bytes restored. | Reverted |
| `skill_not_found` | No id matched. `near` lists similar ids. | No |
| `name_ambiguous` | The name matched several skills. `candidates` lists ids. | No |
| `missing_param` | Neither `id` nor `name` was given. | No |

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "action": "disable",
  "ok": false,
  "warnings": [],
  "error": { "code": "verification_failed", "message": "回读校验失败（期望 deny，实际 allow）；已回滚，文件未留下半成品。" },
  "id": "windows-shell",
  "effect": "deny",
  "changed": false,
  "rolledBack": true
}
```

## Soft disable

`effect: "ask"` keeps the skill in the model-visible list. Every load asks for confirmation.
It is useful when you want the skill available but not silently invoked.

If the caller is already `deny`, `disable` returns `ok: true`, `changed: false`,
`reason: "already_disabled"` and writes nothing — it does not downgrade a deny to `ask`. Run
[`enable`](../enable/) first, then `disable` with `effect: "ask"`. Each successful call appends
one rule; the newest rule for the same id wins.

## Writes configuration?

Yes, unless `dryRun: true`. Only the global config's `permissions` array is edited. Project
config, agent-level permissions and policies are out of scope.

Next: [`enable`](../enable/) reverses it.

---
title: enable
description: Delete the one exact global rule that blocks a skill — or refuse with a JSON error code and show why it cannot be uniquely identified.
---

`enable` removes the blocking rule from the global config. It does not add an `allow` rule: once
the exact `deny`/`ask` entry is gone, the skill returns to normal evaluation (and, if nothing
else matches, to the host's `ask` fallback).

The rule does not have to have been written by this tool. It does have to be uniquely
identifiable.

## Parameters

| Name | Type | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `action` | `"enable"` | yes | Selects this action. |
| `id` | string | one of `id` / `name` | Skill to restore. |
| `name` | string | one of `id` / `name` | Alias; only when it matches exactly one skill. |
| `dryRun` | boolean | no | Default `false`. `true` shows what would be deleted and writes nothing. |

```text
skill_management({ action: "enable", id: "windows-shell" })
skill_management({ action: "enable", id: "windows-shell", dryRun: true })
```

## Which rules are candidates

Only rules that:

- have `resource` exactly equal to the skill id,
- have `effect` `deny` or `ask`,
- have an `action` that glob-matches `skill`.

`allow` rules are not blockers and are never deleted. Wildcard resources, agent-level
`permissions` and policies are not candidates either; they are reported only.

## How the rule is identified

1. **Same-line marker comment.** A rule ending in `// skill_management` is self-identifying,
   even if the sidecar is gone. This is the normal path.
2. **Sidecar record, no marker.** If `<config>/skill_management.state.json` records the id and
   the config contains exactly one identical rule, that rule is deleted with a warning that the
   marker was stripped.
3. **Neither.** It refuses, returns the exact rule text from the config, and leaves the file
   alone. It does not guess which of several similar rules you meant.

It also refuses when the config cannot be parsed, because locating and safely deleting a rule
from malformed JSONC is not possible.

## When it cannot help

If the caller is blocked but there is no exact rule for the id, `enable` explains that the
blocker is not "this line":

- a wildcard or otherwise broader `skill` rule,
- an agent-level rule in `agents.<id>.permissions`,
- `policies` / `experimental.policies`, which the plugin cannot read (its context has no
  `config` domain).

Those cases are reported with the matched rule, never edited. Fix them by hand.

## What happens, in order

1. Resolve the skill and the caller's current effect.
2. Read the target config plus any file recorded in the sidecar.
3. Locate the candidate exact rule(s) and choose a unique one as described above.
4. Remove the item — and the `permissions` block if this edit made it empty.
5. Write atomically, preserving indentation, key order, EOL and BOM; keep one backup.
6. Reload and poll until the caller's exact-rule count decreases, or time out
   (`SKILL_MGMT_VERIFY_TIMEOUT_MS`, default 6 s). On timeout, restore the original bytes.
7. Report the rule's origin and the caller's **post-deletion** effective effect. If a broader
   rule still denies it, the result says so instead of implying success.

## What it returns

The usual envelope (`schemaVersion`, `action`, `ok`, `warnings`) plus:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `id`, `dryRun` | string, boolean | Echo of the resolved request. |
| `callerAgent` | string \| null | Agent whose rule set was used. |
| `before` | object | `index` and `rule` before deletion; `rule` is `null` when nothing matched. |
| `targetFiles` | string[] | Files considered (target config plus any sidecar-recorded file). |
| `changed` | boolean | `true` only when a rule was actually deleted. |
| `reason` | string | Present when `changed` is `false`: `nothing_to_enable`. |
| `message` | string | The human-readable explanation for a no-op or a `dryRun`. |
| `location` | object | `how` = `marker` or `sidecar`; `origin` is the prose explanation. |
| `rule` | object | `file` and the exact `text` of the deleted (or deletable) rule. |
| `diff` | string[] | The removed line, for `dryRun`. |
| `backup` | string | Backup path for the file that was edited. |
| `sidecar` | string \| null | Sidecar path written after success; `null` when the sidecar could not be written (the deletion still stands and `warnings` explains the stale record). |
| `verification` | object | `ok`, `via`, `caller`, and `effect` after deletion. |

A successful run also reports whether a now-empty `permissions` block was cleaned up, and if the
caller is still `deny` because of a broader rule, that rule is quoted in `warnings`.

## Errors

| `error.code` | When | Extra fields |
|---|---|---|
| `unverifiable_origin` | Neither marker nor sidecar confirms the rule. | `rule`: the exact line |
| `ambiguous_rule` | Several exact rules for the same id. | `candidates[]`: `file`, `text` |
| `no_matching_rule` | No exact rule; the blocker is broader. | `relatedRules[]`, `callerHit` |
| `config_unparsable` | The target config has a JSONC syntax error. | `warnings` |
| `verification_failed` | The host did not drop the rule in time. | `rolledBack: true` |
| `skill_not_found` / `name_ambiguous` / `missing_param` | Target resolution failed. | `near` / `candidates` |

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "action": "enable",
  "ok": false,
  "warnings": [],
  "error": {
    "code": "ambiguous_rule",
    "message": "拒绝执行：配置里有 2 条精确命中 `windows-shell` 的规则，无法唯一定位（宿主求值是最后一条命中算数）。"
  },
  "id": "windows-shell",
  "changed": false,
  "candidates": [
    { "file": "<config>\\opencode.jsonc", "text": "{ \"action\": \"skill\", \"resource\": \"windows-shell\", \"effect\": \"deny\" } // skill_management" },
    { "file": "<config>\\opencode.jsonc", "text": "{ \"action\": \"skill\", \"resource\": \"windows-shell\", \"effect\": \"deny\" }" }
  ]
}
```

## Outcome at a glance

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Rule written by this tool, marker intact | `ok: true`, `location.how = "marker"`. |
| Marker stripped, sidecar matches one rule | `ok: true`, `location.how = "sidecar"`, warning to check the config. |
| Two identical rules for the same id | `ok: false`, `ambiguous_rule`, candidates printed. |
| Blocked by `resource: "*"` | `ok: false`, `no_matching_rule`, broad rule in `relatedRules`. |
| Blocked only in one agent's own rules | `ok: false`, `no_matching_rule`, `callerHit` names the agent. |
| No rule and not blocked | `ok: true`, `changed: false`, `reason: "nothing_to_enable"`. |

## Writes configuration?

Yes, unless `dryRun: true`, and only when a unique exact rule is found. A refusal writes
nothing.

Next: read [Permissions & evaluation](../../permissions/) to understand what happens after the
rule is gone.

---
title: inspect
description: One skill in detail — conclusion, matched rule, per-agent differences and where the id came from. Read-only, JSON output.
---

`inspect` is the diagnostic action. It answers three questions about one skill: is it usable
right now, which rule decided that, and why does that rule apply to this id?

It is read-only.

## Parameters

| Name | Type | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `action` | `"inspect"` | yes | Selects this action. |
| `id` | string | one of `id` / `name` | Skill id. Exact match. |
| `name` | string | one of `id` / `name` | Alias. Used only when `id` does not match, and only if it hits exactly one skill. |

`id` wins when both are supplied. A `name` that matches several skills does not guess: it
returns the candidate ids.

```text
skill_management({ action: "inspect", id: "windows-shell" })
skill_management({ action: "inspect", name: "windows-shell" })
```

## What it returns

The same envelope as every action (`schemaVersion`, `action`, `ok`, `warnings`), plus:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `matchedBy` | string | `id` or `name`. |
| `skill.id` | string \| null | Resolved skill id. |
| `skill.name` | string \| null | Registry name. |
| `skill.nameDiffersFromId` | boolean | Whether `frontmatter.name` overrides the id. |
| `skill.path` | string \| null | Path from the registry. |
| `skill.source` / `skill.scope` | string | Same values as `list`. |
| `skill.description` | string \| null | First line of the registry description. |
| `skill.autoinvoke` | boolean \| null | Registry value, or `null` when not provided. |
| `skill.frontmatter` | object | `name` and `disableModelInvocation`, each string/boolean or `null` when unreadable. |
| `idDerivation.idSource` | string | `registry`, `derived` or `none`. |
| `idDerivation.explained` | string | Which rule produced the id, in prose. |
| `idDerivation.rule` | string \| null | The derivation rule text. |
| `idDerivation.pathField` | string \| null | Which registry field was used as the path (`path` or `location`). |
| `idDerivation.dir` / `idDerivation.base` | string \| null | Inputs to the derivation. |
| `agents[]` | object[] | Per-agent evaluation: `id`, `effect`, `index`, `rule` (`null` when no rule matched). |
| `divergentAgents[]` | object[] | Agents whose effect differs from the caller's: `id`, `effect`. |
| `caller` | object | `id`, `effect`, `index`, `rule`, `coveredByBroaderRule`, `broaderRule`. |
| `conclusion.state` | string | `available`, `disabled` or `ask`. |
| `conclusion.message` | string | The same conclusion as one human-readable sentence. |

`index` is the position of the last matching rule in that agent's rule set; `-1` means no rule
matched and the host fell back to `ask`. Missing values are `null`, never invented.

### id derivation

If the registry supplied an `id`, `idSource` is `registry` and the path is included for
cross-checking. If it did not, the id was derived from the path:

- `<dir>/SKILL.md` → the directory name.
- `<dir>/<name>.md` → the file name without `.md`.

If neither an id nor a usable path exists, `idSource` is `none`, `rule` is `null`, and the id is
treated as empty.

### Per-agent evaluation

`agents` is the per-agent answer that `list` points to when it says other agents disagree. It is
not merged: each entry is evaluated against that agent's own final rule set.

### The conclusion

- `disabled` — effect `deny`; the skill is hidden from the model-visible list and loading is
  rejected.
- `ask` — effect `ask`; still listed, confirmation on load.
- `available` — any non-blocking effect.

When the caller is denied by a wildcard or other broader rule (the matched `resource` is not this
skill's id), `caller.coveredByBroaderRule` is `true` and `caller.broaderRule` holds that rule:
the skill is blocked, but adding a rule for this id would not be the fix.

## Errors

| `error.code` | When |
|---|---|
| `skill_not_found` | No id matched. `near` lists similar ids from the registry. |
| `name_ambiguous` | The name matched several skills. `candidates` lists their ids. |

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "action": "inspect",
  "ok": false,
  "warnings": [],
  "error": { "code": "skill_not_found", "message": "未找到 skill `no-such-skill`。（结论来自实际读到的注册表，未做猜测）" },
  "near": ["windows-shell"]
}
```

## Example output

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "action": "inspect",
  "ok": true,
  "warnings": [],
  "matchedBy": "id",
  "skill": {
    "id": "windows-shell",
    "name": "windows-shell",
    "nameDiffersFromId": false,
    "path": "<config>\\skills\\windows-shell\\SKILL.md",
    "source": "config",
    "scope": "user",
    "description": "Windows shell conventions…",
    "autoinvoke": null,
    "frontmatter": { "name": "windows-shell", "disableModelInvocation": null }
  },
  "idDerivation": {
    "idSource": "registry",
    "pathField": "path",
    "dir": "<config>\\skills\\windows-shell",
    "base": "SKILL.md",
    "rule": "<dir>/SKILL.md → 取 SKILL.md 所在目录名",
    "explained": "注册表直接给出（本工具不反推，仅列出对应规则供核对）"
  },
  "agents": [
    { "id": "build", "effect": "deny", "index": 3, "rule": { "action": "skill", "resource": "windows-shell", "effect": "deny" } },
    { "id": "explorer", "effect": "allow", "index": 0, "rule": { "action": "skill", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" } }
  ],
  "divergentAgents": [{ "id": "explorer", "effect": "allow" }],
  "caller": {
    "id": "build",
    "effect": "deny",
    "index": 3,
    "rule": { "action": "skill", "resource": "windows-shell", "effect": "deny" },
    "coveredByBroaderRule": false,
    "broaderRule": null
  },
  "conclusion": {
    "state": "disabled",
    "message": "`windows-shell` 对调用者 agent `build` 当前不可用：权限效果为 deny（命中 rules[3] = {\"action\":\"skill\",\"resource\":\"windows-shell\",\"effect\":\"deny\"}），模型可见列表会隐藏它、且 skill 工具加载会被拒。"
  }
}
```

## When to use it

- `list` shows `ask` and you need to know whether a rule says `ask` or nothing matched.
- A skill is installed but the model cannot load it.
- `disable` reported that the rule was written but the caller still sees a different effect.
- Before `enable`, to confirm which rule is actually blocking.

Next: [`disable`](../disable/) to act on what you found.

---
title: list
description: Every registered skill, its effective state for the calling agent, and config consistency notes. Read-only, JSON output.
---

`list` answers "what is installed right now, and which of it is actually available to me?"

It is read-only. It writes no files and changes no configuration.

## Parameters

| Name | Type | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `action` | `"list"` | yes | Selects this action. |
| other fields | — | no | Ignored by `list`. `id`, `name`, `effect` and `dryRun` are not used. |

```text
skill_management({ action: "list" })
```

## What it returns

One JSON object. Every action starts with the same envelope:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `schemaVersion` | number | `1` in 1.2.x. |
| `action` | string | `"list"`. |
| `ok` | boolean | `true` when the registry and config were read. |
| `warnings` | string[] | Human-readable notes (Chinese in 1.2.x); empty when there is nothing to report. |

`list` adds:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `callerAgent.id` | string \| null | Agent whose rule set was evaluated. |
| `callerAgent.verified` | boolean | `false` when `context.agent` was missing or not in the registry; the result falls back to a visible agent and `warnings` says so. |
| `summary.total` | number | Registered skills. |
| `summary.disabled` | number | Skills whose caller effect is `deny`. |
| `summary.ask` | number | Skills whose caller effect is `ask` (explicit or host fallback). |
| `summary.diverged` | number | Skills whose effect differs under at least one other **visible** agent. `hidden` internal agents (`title`, `summary`, …) are excluded; their detail is still in `inspect.agents[]`. |
| `summary.derivedIds` | number | Ids derived from paths because the registry supplied none. |
| `skills[]` | object[] | One entry per skill, sorted by id. |
| `skills[].id` | string \| null | Registry id, or derived from the path. `null` when neither exists. |
| `skills[].name` | string \| null | Registry name (`frontmatter.name` when it differs). |
| `skills[].autoinvoke` | boolean \| null | `false` means the registry turned auto-invocation off; `null` when the registry did not provide it. |
| `skills[].source` | string | `embedded`, `config`, `claude`, `agents`, `catalog`, `project`, `plugin` or `unknown`. |
| `skills[].scope` | string | `user` or `project`, relative to the home directory. |
| `skills[].state` | string | `available`, `disabled`, `ask` or `unknown`. Evaluated for the **calling agent only**. |
| `skills[].path` | string \| null | Absolute path as reported by the registry. |
| `skills[].description` | string \| null | First line of the description; not truncated further. |
| `config.file` | string | Global config file that writes would target. |
| `config.configDir` | string | Resolved `<config>` directory. |
| `config.configDirs` | string[] | Candidate directories considered. |
| `config.hadPermissions` | boolean | Whether the target document already had a `permissions` array. |
| `config.notes` | string[] | Why that file was chosen. |
| `sidecar.file` | string | `<config>/skill_management.state.json`. |
| `sidecar.ok` | boolean | Whether the sidecar could be read. |
| `sidecar.error` | string \| null | Read error, without guessing at its meaning. |
| `consistency.staleSidecarIds` | string[] | Sidecar records with no matching rule in the config. |
| `consistency.unrecordedRules` | object[] | Config `skill` rules the sidecar does not know: `resource`, `effect`. |
| `consistency.missingFromRegistry` | string[] | Recorded ids that are no longer registered. |

Skill bodies are never included. Messages inside `warnings` are Chinese in 1.2.x; field names and
values above are the stable part.

## Reading `state`

- `available` — the caller's last matching rule is `allow`, or an earlier rule allows it and
  nothing overrides it.
- `disabled` — the last matching rule is `deny`. The skill is hidden from the model-visible list
  and loading it is rejected.
- `ask` — the last matching rule is `ask`, **or no rule matched at all** (the host falls back to
  `ask`). `list` cannot tell those two cases apart; use [`inspect`](../inspect/).

State is computed per agent on purpose. Merging all agents' rules would leak a sub-agent's
`deny` into the caller's view, which is a bug this project has already had to fix.

## Example output

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "action": "list",
  "ok": true,
  "warnings": ["另有 2 个 skill 在其它可见 agent 下状态不同（逐 agent 明细见 inspect）。"],
  "callerAgent": { "id": "build", "verified": true },
  "summary": { "total": 29, "disabled": 1, "ask": 0, "diverged": 2, "derivedIds": 0 },
  "skills": [
    {
      "id": "windows-shell",
      "name": "windows-shell",
      "autoinvoke": null,
      "source": "config",
      "scope": "user",
      "state": "available",
      "path": "<config>\\skills\\windows-shell\\SKILL.md",
      "description": "Windows shell conventions…"
    },
    {
      "id": "pdf-tools",
      "name": "pdf-tools",
      "autoinvoke": null,
      "source": "catalog",
      "scope": "user",
      "state": "disabled",
      "path": "<cache>\\skills\\pdf-tools\\SKILL.md",
      "description": "Read and extract from PDF files."
    }
  ],
  "config": {
    "file": "<config>\\opencode.jsonc",
    "configDir": "<config>",
    "configDirs": ["<config>"],
    "hadPermissions": true,
    "notes": ["目标文件含现有 permissions，直接在其数组中追加/删除"]
  },
  "sidecar": { "file": "<config>\\skill_management.state.json", "ok": true, "error": null },
  "consistency": { "staleSidecarIds": [], "unrecordedRules": [], "missingFromRegistry": [] }
}
```

Use it before a bulk cleanup, and again after `disable` to confirm the state actually changed.

Next: [`inspect`](../inspect/) when a row surprises you.

---
title: 兼容性与 1.x 承诺
description: 宿主与运行时支持范围、1.x 内不破坏什么，以及明确不在范围内的部分。
---

## 支持矩阵

| 面 | 状态 |
|---|---|
| OpenCode V2 | 支持。1.1.0 在宿主 **2.0.32** 上完成验收（Windows + Linux）；1.2.x 在宿主 **2.2.0** 上用新进程复核（Windows），包含并发写操作。 |
| OpenCode V1 | 不针对，未测试。 |
| Windows | 已验证，包含新进程端到端。 |
| Linux | 已验证，包含新进程端到端。 |
| Node.js | **18 或更新**（插件运行在宿主进程内）。 |
| 运行时依赖 | 无。纯 Node 内置模块。 |
| shell 调用 | 无。 |
| 插件结构 | 单文件。 |

## 1.x 兼容承诺

在 1.x 内，以下内容不会以破坏性方式改变：

1. 四个动作（`list`、`inspect`、`disable`、`enable`）及其入参字段。
2. **JSON 结果信封**：`schemaVersion`、`action`、`ok`、`warnings`，以及 1.1.0 文档里写明的
   各动作字段。可以新增字段，但不会删除或改变已有字段的含义。
3. 写入的规则形状：
   `{ "action": "skill", "resource": <id>, "effect": "deny" | "ask" }`。
4. 行尾标记注释格式（`// skill_management`）。sidecar 丢失后，`enable` 靠它确认来源。
5. 单文件插件结构。

**1.1.0 是破坏性版本。** 它把 1.0.0 的 Markdown 输出换成了每次调用一个 JSON 对象。这是自
1.0.0 以来唯一的破坏性变更：动作、入参、规则形状、标记格式与文件结构都没变。

消息措辞不属于契约。1.1.0 中 `warnings`、`message`、`conclusion.message`、`error.message`
里的人类可读文字是中文；稳定的是信封、字段名与字面量（id、效果、规则 JSON、路径）。

## 「支持」不意味着

- **项目级配置不在范围内。** 项目可以有自己的 permissions。本插件只读写全局配置，并在
  `config.file` 里报告全局目标文件。
- **`policies` 不在范围内。** 插件上下文没有 `config` 域，读不到 policy 文档。policy 挡住某个
  skill 时，`enable` 只报告然后停下。
- **agent 级规则只读不写。** 它们出现在 `inspect.agents[]` 里，也可能对某个 agent 覆盖全局
  规则。工具会如实报告，而不是「顺手修好」。
- **宿主注册表内部接口属于内部实现。** 插件通过宿主的 transform API 读取 `ctx.skill` /
  `ctx.agent`，必要时消费 `{ location, data }` 信封。宿主改变这些形状属于兼容性事件，
  插件无法单方面抹平。
- **无网络访问。** 插件不向外请求；文档站也没有分析、cookie 或按语言跳转。

## 这一版是怎么验的

- `node tools/verify.mjs`：A–J 共 **333 项断言**，全部跑在临时配置目录（不碰真实用户配置）。
  E 段把每个结果都解析出来，并按声明的 `output` 契约校验。
- 同一套断言在 CI 的 `ubuntu-latest` 与 `windows-latest` 上运行。
- 端到端在**新进程**里跑，因为插件在宿主启动时加载。
- H 段是性能闸门：29 skills × 12 agents × 10 rules 下 `list` < 25 ms。
- I 段是发布闸门：打包内容、`exports` 可解析、安装副本逐字节一致。

细节与 Linux/WSL 验收脚本见[开发与验收](../development/)。

这些检查针对插件。文档站用 Astro + Starlight 单独构建，部署到 GitHub Pages。

## 升级

- patch 版本修行为，不改上面的接口。
- minor 版本可以增加输出字段，但不会删除或改变已有字段的含义。1.1.0 是文档里写明的例外：
  Markdown 输出被 JSON 取代。
- 宿主升级导致注册表或重载行为变化时，插件会写「未验证」，而不是编一个结论。不要用「没有报错」
  推断「已支持」。

## 版本

当前版本 **1.2.1**。npm 包名 `opencode-skill-management`，仓库
[sogeisetsu/opencode-skill-management](https://github.com/sogeisetsu/opencode-skill-management)。
MIT 许可。

---
title: 设计取舍
description: 为什么写 permission 规则而不是 policy、为什么不提供 allow、为什么按文本最小编辑，以及每个选择的代价。
---

`skill_management` 是刻意做小的：四个动作、一种规则形状、一个允许写的文件。这一页记录这些
选择、它们的证据，以及每个选择的**代价**。

## 为什么写 `permissions` 规则，而不是 `policies` 条目

OpenCode 有两种方式阻止一个 skill 被使用：

| 机制 | 去掉了什么 | 粒度 | 本工具能写吗 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `permissions` 规则，`effect: "deny"` | 从模型可见列表里消失，加载被拒 | 单个 skill id，**按 agent** | 能 |
| `policies`（`integration.use` deny） | 把 skill 从注册表里摘掉 | 单个 integration id，全局 | 不能 |

选权限规则，是因为它是唯一能表达本工具必须区分的三种状态的机制：`allow`、`deny`、`ask`。
`ask` 是宿主原生的 `Permission.Effect`，不是变通：skill 仍在列表里，加载时才询问。规则也按
每个 agent 自己的规则集求值，所以工具能回答「**对我**可用吗」这种按 agent 的问题，而不是
一个全局结论。

**代价。** policy 的 deny 更彻底：它把 skill 从注册表摘掉（`s.remove(id)`），对所有 agent 都
消失，连直接读注册表的工具也看不到。本工具做不到这一点，也读不到 policy 文档 —— 插件上下文
没有 `config` 域。如果挡住某个 skill 的是 policy，`enable` 只报告然后停下。

想让一个 skill 对所有人都不存在，用 policy；想要一个可见、按 agent 生效、可撤销的开关，用权限规则。

## 为什么不提供 `allow`

`disable` 只追加 `deny` 或 `ask`；`enable` 只删除效果为这两者之一的规则。

追加一条 `allow` 会在该 id 上优先于所有更早的规则，包括别人故意写的更宽的 `deny`。那等于
工具为了「修好」一个 skill，去覆盖一个它从未参与的决定，影响范围被悄悄放大。它还会破坏归属
模型：`enable` 靠效果与标记认出自己写的规则，一条自己写的 `allow` 就成了没人回收的规则。

**代价。** 恢复永远是「删除」，不是「覆盖」。如果删完仍被 agent 级规则或通配 `deny` 挡住，
工具只报告，不动手 —— 那条规则由你改。

## 为什么只写全局配置

写入目标只有一个，按写明的顺序解析（见[权限规则与求值模型](../permissions/#写哪个配置文件)）。
项目级配置、`agents.<id>.permissions` 与 `policies` 只读或只报告，绝不代改。

只有一个目标，工具才能对自己改了什么保持诚实：`config.file` 点名它，备份取自它，`enable`
先在它里面找。也意味着不会在你碰巧所在的项目里留下意外改动。

**代价。** 不能只对某个项目停用，也不能只对某个 agent 停用。两者都是真实需求，都不在范围内。

## 为什么按文本最小编辑，并带同行标记

全局配置通常是手工维护的 JSONC：注释、键顺序、缩进、CRLF/LF，有时还有 BOM。解析成对象再
序列化回去会毁掉这些，所以插件按文本插入或删除那一条，写前再校验结果。

行尾的 `// skill_management` 注释是**文件内**的来源信息。sidecar 丢失或损坏时它还在，
`enable` 首先找它。它的格式属于 1.x 兼容承诺 —— sidecar 丢失后能删掉规则，靠的就是它。

**代价。** 写出去的标记格式永远不能变。另外，如果别的工具把配置里的注释剥掉了，标记就没了：
`enable` 会退回 sidecar 记录，或者拒绝而不是猜着删。

## 为什么写操作要串行

宿主会把同一个 step 里的多个工具调用**并发**执行。两个写操作同时改一个文件时，
「读 → 改 → 回读校验 → 记录」会交错：后一个的回滚可能把前一个刚写入的规则写回去，
文件里最后留下一条本不该存在的规则。

现在每个 `disable` / `enable` 都排进进程内队列：后到的调用要等前一个（包括它的回读轮询）
走完才真正开始，于是它读到的必然是前一个的结果。

**代价。** 后到的写是「等待」而不是「被拒绝」，而回读校验可能要好几秒，所以并发调用会被推迟
这么久。队列只覆盖单个宿主进程：两个 OpenCode 进程同时改同一份配置仍可能互相覆盖，
那不是插件能锁住的范围。

## 为什么 sidecar 只是审计线索

`<config>/skill_management.state.json` 记录本工具写过的规则的 id、效果、文件与时间戳。它
从不被「重放」：与配置不一致时，`list` 报告差异，以配置为准。

**代价。** 标记和 sidecar 记录都丢了，`enable` 就无法证明这条规则是本工具写的，只能把原文
打印出来。写 sidecar 也是尽力而为：写不进去时配置改动仍算完成，结果里 `sidecar` 为 `null`，
`warnings` 写明原因。

## 按场景选机制

| 你想要 | 用什么 |
|---|---|
| 对所有 agent 都消失，像没装过一样 | `policies`（`integration.use` deny） |
| 对当前 agent 隐藏，并在加载时拒绝 | `disable`（`permissions` 规则，`effect: "deny"`） |
| 保留在列表里，每次加载都确认 | `disable` + `effect: "ask"` |
| 不自动进上下文，但仍能按名字加载 | `SKILL.md` 的 `disable-model-invocation` —— 那是 frontmatter，不是权限；本工具只报告 |

下一步：[开发与验收](../development/)，看这些行为是怎么被测出来的。

---
title: 开发与验收
description: 验收脚本的分段与闸门、CI 矩阵、npm 包里有什么，以及为什么两份插件不能并存。
---

仓库没有测试框架，也没有构建步骤。整套验收就是一个 Node 脚本，跑在临时配置目录上。

## 跑验收

```pwsh
node tools/verify.mjs                # 全量，333 项断言
node tools/verify.mjs --section E    # 只跑一段（A–J，按标题前缀匹配，大小写不敏感）
node tools/verify.mjs --keep         # 不删除临时目录（排查用）
```

每次运行都会新建 `mkdtemp` 目录并把 `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` 指过去，所以真实全局配置既不被读也
不被写。安装器那一步也有自己的临时 `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`，并且清掉 `OPENCODE_CONFIG` /
`OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR`，避免把正在运行的实例的 npm 渠道误判成本机已装。

## 分段

| 段 | 覆盖 |
|---|---|
| A | 模块形状与纯度：default export、四个动作、只 import `node:`、无第三方依赖、不调用 shell / `eval` |
| B | `globMatch` 与权限求值：后匹配者胜，无命中回退 `ask` |
| C | 从路径反推 id、来源归类、`user` / `project` 作用域 |
| D | JSONC 文本编辑：插入、删除、新建块、CRLF、BOM、保留注释、严格校验、失败路径 |
| D2 | 用假 `env` / `home` 测目标文件解析：XDG、家目录、两个候选、两个目录 |
| E | 临时配置上的端到端：`list`、`inspect`、`dryRun`、`disable`、`enable`、备份、sidecar、回读校验、拒绝分支、同一文件的并发写，以及按 `OUTPUT_SCHEMA` 校验每个动作的 `output` |
| F | 从注册表反推 id（§3.5）与 `enable` 的归属边界 |
| G | 回读判据、只留一份备份、原子写、description 硬化 |
| H | 性能闸门 |
| I | 发布闸门 |
| J | 安装器冲突检测 |

E 段会把每个结果解析出来，按声明的 `output` schema 校验：必需字段、属性类型、`error.code` /
`error.message`，并断言 `content` 与 `output` 是同一份数据。它的负向用例保证校验器不是空转：
声明为 string 的位置塞 `null`、声明为 boolean 的位置塞字符串，都必须被报出来。

## Linux / WSL

```bash
bash tools/linux-verify.sh      # KEEP=1 保留临时目录
```

这是真宿主验收，不是单元测试。脚本自己下载 Node 与 `@opencode/cli`（版本由 `NODE_VERSION` /
`OPENCODE_VERSION` 固定），在仓库副本上跑验收，然后在临时 `HOME` 里加载插件并检查
`opencode plugin list --builtin`。需要 `curl`、`tar`、`gzip`，不需要 `sudo`，退出时删掉临时
目录。它还会在跑前跑后各拍一次真实 `~/.config/opencode` 与 `~/.local/share/opencode` 的快照，
被改过就报失败。

## CI

`.github/workflows/verify.yml` 在 `ubuntu-latest` 与 `windows-latest` 上用 Node 22 跑
`node tools/verify.mjs`。不需要任何 secret：全程不碰真实配置。
`.github/workflows/pages.yml` 构建文档站并跑 `npm run docs:check` —— 少路由、en/zh 路由不镜像、
站内死链、超出 base 的链接、语言切换不指向镜像页，都会让它失败。

## 两个闸门

**H —— 性能。** 29 skills × 12 agents × 10 rules，`list` 五次取最快，必须低于 25 ms。阈值刻意
放宽，避免 CI 抖动误报；它的作用是抓住意外的 O(n²) 或「每个 skill 重解析一次配置」。

**I —— 发布。** `npm pack --dry-run` 必须包含入口文件，且不含 `tools/`、`docs/`、CI 或仓库文档；
`exports["."]` 必须能按包名解析；安装出来的单文件副本必须与 `src/skill_management.js` 逐字节一致。

## npm 包里有什么

只有 5 个文件：

```text
package.json
README.md
CHANGELOG.md
LICENSE
src/skill_management.js
```

`package.json` 写了 `files: ["src", "CHANGELOG.md"]`，npm 再补 `package.json`、`README.md`、
`LICENSE`。测试、文档站、CI 与设计规范都留在仓库里。

## 为什么插件是单文件

宿主会把 `<config>/plugins/` 下的每个 `.js` / `.ts` 文件（含子目录）都当插件加载。把辅助模块
拆出去会变成第二个插件，校验直接失败。所以发布形态就是单文件，`tools/install.mjs` 复制的也
是这一份。

同理，两份不能并存：npm 条目与 `<config>/plugins/skill_management.js` 同时存在时，宿主报
`Duplicate plugin ID: skill_management`，其中一份显示为加载失败 —— 不是「两份都能用、只是忽略
一份」。切渠道用 `node tools/install.mjs --uninstall`（切到 npm）或
`opencode plugin remove opencode-skill-management`（切回单文件），改之前先跑
`node tools/install.mjs --check` 看清两处来源。

下一步：[设计取舍](../design-decisions/)，看这些行为为什么值得被这样测。

---
title: 安装
description: 三条加载通道（npm、git spec、单文件）以及如何确认插件已加载。
---

插件是一个 JavaScript 文件，没有第三方运行时依赖。任选一条通道，落到磁盘上的都是同一份代码。

## 环境要求

- OpenCode **V2**。1.1.0 在宿主 2.0.32 上完成验收（Windows 与 Linux）；1.2.x 在 2.2.0 上复核，包含新进程端到端。
- 运行 OpenCode 的环境需要 Node.js **18 或更新版本**。
- 不需要 token、注册表账号或构建步骤。

## 通道一 —— npm（推荐）

```pwsh
opencode plugin add opencode-skill-management
```

没有特别理由就用这条：一条命令装包并登记到全局配置，升级交给宿主（`opencode plugin check` /
`opencode plugin update`）。npm 包只导出一个入口：`./src/skill_management.js`。运行时依赖：无。

## 通道二 —— git spec

```pwsh
opencode plugin add github:sogeisetsu/opencode-skill-management
```

OpenCode 直接拉取仓库，不经过 npm 注册表，也没有发布环节；升级同样走宿主的
`opencode plugin check` / `opencode plugin update`。

## 通道三 —— 直接复制单文件（不跟 npm 更新）

离线机器或自建分发更适合这条通道：

```pwsh
node tools/install.mjs          # 复制到 <config>/plugins/skill_management.js
node tools/install.mjs --check  # 只报告：落点、版本、有没有冲突
```

这条通道是**锁版本**的：装进去的那份一直用到你重新跑安装器为止。它不跟 npm 发布走，升级就是再跑
一次 `node tools/install.mjs`。想要自动更新就用通道一或通道二，升级交给宿主的
`opencode plugin check` / `opencode plugin update`。

`<config>` 的解析顺序与宿主一致：`$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` → `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode` →
`~/.config/opencode`（Windows 上是 `C:\Users\<你>\.config\opencode`）。

写任何文件之前，安装器先看有没有第二个来源。`opencode.json(c)` 的 `plugins` 里已经列了本包，
或者 `plugins/` 里还躺着另一份副本时，它拒绝写入、返回退出码 `2`，所有文件保持原样。

| 参数 | 作用 |
|---|---|
| `--check` / `--dry-run` | 只报告，不写任何文件 |
| `--uninstall` | 只删 `<config>/plugins/skill_management.js`（内容不像本插件就拒绝） |
| `--npm` | 断言走 npm 渠道，永不写文件；没找到渠道退出 `1` |
| `--force` | 无视冲突照写（会制造两份，宿主会给其中一份报 `Duplicate plugin ID`） |
| `--json` | 机器可读输出 |
| `--help` / `-h` | 打印用法并退出 `0`；不写任何文件 |

未知参数退出 `3`，不写任何文件。

OpenCode 会加载 `<config>/plugins/` 下的每个 `.js`、`.ts` 文件以及子目录。不需要在
`opencode.jsonc` 里登记。

:::caution[插件目录必须保持单文件]
`plugins/` 下的每个文件都会被当成插件加载。不要把 `skill_management` 拆成辅助模块，也不要
在旁边放第二份副本。分发形态刻意保持单文件，原因就在这里。
:::

:::caution[一份插件只能走一条通道]
同一个 plugin id 只能被加载一次。npm 条目和 `<config>/plugins/skill_management.js` 同时存在时，
宿主会报 `Duplicate plugin ID: skill_management`，其中一份显示为加载失败——不是“两份都能用”。
改走 npm：先 `node tools/install.mjs --uninstall`。改回单文件：先
`opencode plugin remove opencode-skill-management`。拿不准先跑
`node tools/install.mjs --check`，它会列出两处来源和该跑哪条命令。
:::

## 确认已加载

```pwsh
opencode plugin list --builtin
```

`--builtin` 不能省。不带它时，本地目录加载的插件不会出现在列表里，可能显示
`No plugins found`。

输出里应出现 `skill_management`：单文件通道显示 `local`，npm / git spec 显示包来源。全新的配置
目录里，前两次调用可能为空，再跑一次即可。

然后让模型调用工具，或自己调用：

```text
skill_management({ action: "list" })
```

`list` 返回里的 `config.file` 与 `skills[]`，足以确认插件读到了宿主注册表。

## 加载说明

- 插件在 OpenCode 进程启动时加载。新装的插件出现在下一个进程里，不会出现在已经运行的进程里。
- `skill_management` 注册为**原生工具**，`codemode: false`。直接按名字调用；它不在 Code Mode
  的 `search()` / `execute()` 目录里，「那里找不到」不等于没装上。
- 工具只写全局配置，绝不写项目配置。

装好后继续看[概览](../overview/)，或直接进入 [`list`](../actions/list/)。

---
title: 概览
description: opencode-skill-management 做什么、为什么用权限规则承载状态，以及它刻意不碰什么。
---

`opencode-skill-management` 是一个单文件的 OpenCode V2 插件。它注册一个原生工具
`skill_management`，包含四个动作：`list`、`inspect`、`disable`、`enable`。

它不安装、不删除、不移动、不改写任何 skill。它读取宿主当前的注册表；当你要求改动时，
只向全局 OpenCode 配置写入**一条精确的权限规则**。

## 它解决什么问题

**skill 列表变成噪音。** 每个已安装 skill 都会把名称和描述注入模型上下文。列表一长，
真正有用的条目更难被看见，而每一轮都要为其余部分付出代价。

**加载失败是个黑盒。** 一个 skill 可以已注册却在加载时被拒。此时关键问题不是「装没装」，
而是「哪条规则、对哪个 agent、在当前这一刻命中了」—— 答案通常要翻三层配置。

**停用一个 skill 的成本过高。** 改目录名或编辑 `SKILL.md` 当然有效，但那是真实的文件改动，
撤回时还得凭记忆。权限规则更小、可读、可逆。

## 模型

OpenCode 把 skill 权限当作规则列表求值，后匹配者胜，支持 glob。插件把这个规则当作它
唯一拥有的状态：

```jsonc
{ "action": "skill", "resource": "windows-shell", "effect": "deny" } // skill_management
```

- `disable` 在全局配置中追加这一条规则。
- `enable` 删除这一条规则。
- 两者都会让宿主重载，然后重新读取调用者 agent 的有效规则集来校验。宿主没有读入的写入
  会回滚，不会被报告成成功。

其余设计都由这一点推出：

| 性质 | 后果 |
|---|---|
| 不碰 skill 文件 | 改主意时没有东西需要恢复 |
| 规则按 agent 求值 | `list` 报告调用者的状态，而不是合并后的全局视图 |
| 无命中回退 `ask` | `ask` 可能是「显式软停用」，也可能是「一条规则都没命中」；`inspect` 会区分 |
| 只写全局配置 | 项目级配置、`policies`、agent 级规则只报告，不修改 |

:::note[输出格式]
每个动作返回一个 JSON 对象：`schemaVersion`、`action`、`ok`、`warnings`，加上本系列页面写明
的动作字段。1.2.x 中 `warnings`、`message`、`conclusion.message`、`error.message` 里的人类
可读文字是中文；字段名与字面量是稳定契约。
:::

## 第一次使用

下面几行是**工具调用**，不是 shell 命令：每一行都是传给原生工具 `skill_management` 的参数对象。

```text title="工具调用"
skill_management({ action: "list" })
skill_management({ action: "inspect", id: "windows-shell" })
skill_management({ action: "disable", id: "windows-shell", dryRun: true })
skill_management({ action: "disable", id: "windows-shell" })
skill_management({ action: "enable",  id: "windows-shell" })
```

`list` 只读，任何时刻都可以跑。两个写动作加 `dryRun` 时只在 `diff` 里返回将要增删的原文，不落盘。

## 它不会做什么

- 编辑、移动、删除、重装 skill，或改 `SKILL.md` frontmatter。
- 写项目级配置。
- 写 `policies` 或 `experimental.policies`。
- 编辑 agent 级 `agents.<id>.permissions`。
- 写 `opencode.managed.json`（OpenChamber 托管的第二份全局配置）。
- 删除一条无法唯一定位的规则。它会贴出候选然后停下。
- 当 agent 级规则仍然覆盖时，把规则说成「已生效」。

## 下一步

- 从三条通道中选一条[安装](../installation/)。
- 逐个看动作：[list](../actions/list/)、[inspect](../actions/inspect/)、
  [disable](../actions/disable/)、[enable](../actions/enable/)。
- 手工改规则前，先读[权限求值模型](../permissions/)。

---
title: 权限规则与求值模型
description: 规则形状、后匹配者胜、ask 回退、agent 级覆盖，以及插件被允许写哪个文件。
---

`skill_management` 改动的全部内容就是一条权限规则。读完这一页，你就能在运行工具之前
预测它会报告什么。

## 规则

